analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicaid to pay for home-based care for people with disabilities instead of nursing homes.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had a bipartisan sponsor group, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on August 1, 2001 and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicaid has a funding bias toward institutional care: federal law guarantees a nursing home bed in every state, but home and community-based help is optional and unevenly available. This bill would have made Medicaid pay for attendant services—help with bathing, dressing, meals, and daily tasks—in a person's own home if they qualify for nursing-home-level care and choose it. States that adopted the benefit early would have gotten a higher federal reimbursement, and grants would help states reorganize their long-term care systems around consumer-controlled home care.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities and older Americans who need nursing-home-level care but want to live at home, their family caregivers, and home care workers, who would see increased demand, better pay, and career prospects under the bill's workforce provisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with disabilities and older Americans

how_it_helps.text: Creates a mandatory Medicaid benefit for community-based attendant services for anyone eligible for nursing facility or intermediate care facility care who chooses to receive services at home instead [S2] [S3].

States that adopt the benefit before October 1, 2005 get an enhanced federal medical assistance percentage for those services, plus a federal match increased by 10 percentage points for activities like one-stop intake, family support, and improving home care worker skills and earnings [S3].

Authorizes $50 million per year for fiscal 2002-2004 in grants to states with a consumer-led task force to build home and community-based care capacity, including transition costs such as first month's rent and deposits for people leaving institutions [S2] [S3].

The bill notes that only about 27 percent of Medicaid long-term care dollars currently pay for home and community-based services, and only 3 states spent 50 percent or more of long-term care funds that way in fiscal 2000 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through higher Medicaid matching payments for home-based services; the nursing home industry, which would lose some residents and revenue as people shifted to home care; and states, which would face new service costs partly offset by the enhanced federal match.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory coverage with an enhanced federal match would significantly increase federal and state Medicaid spending, and states already strained by Medicaid costs in the early 2000s would have to fund and administer a new statewide benefit with quality assurance, abuse reporting, and consumer monitoring systems [S3].

The bill pays federal matching funds for home-based expenditures exceeding 150 percent of the average nursing facility cost, so states could claim federal dollars for home care that costs substantially more than a nursing home placement, raising cost-containment concerns for taxpayers [S3].

A universal entitlement to home care could be difficult to cap or waitlist once enacted, and quality oversight for care delivered in private homes—where workers are less supervised than in facilities—would be harder to enforce despite the bill's monitoring requirements [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and large for a specific group: people with disabilities and older Americans who qualify for nursing home care but want to live independently. The costs are real but moderate—higher Medicaid spending, offset for early-adopting states by an enhanced federal match, and pressure on nursing home revenues. The bill included quality assurance, abuse reporting, and maintenance-of-effort requirements, though a federal entitlement to home care would be hard to scale back once created.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and the 107th Congress ended with the bill dead—no committee vote, no floor vote, no hearing action in the record.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on August 1, 2001, joined by Senators Specter, Kennedy, Biden, and Clinton, with 12 cosponsors total (10 Senate Democrats and 2 Senate Republicans) [S4] [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on August 1, 2001, which was its only committee referral [S1] [S5].
No further action was recorded in the 107th Congress: the Finance Committee never reported the bill, and it never received a floor vote before Congress adjourned on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing homes and institutional long-term care providers are better off, because the federal guarantee of nursing home care remains the default and Medicaid's institutional spending bias was left unchanged. States also avoid new benefit costs and administrative obligations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing homes and institutional care providers

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided: 10 of 49 Senate Democrats and only 2 of 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored, and the Democratic-chaired Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Nursing facilities and institutional long-term care
industries.note: The bill states federal law guarantees only nursing home care in every state, with about 27 percent of Medicaid long-term care dollars going to home and community settings. Mandated home-based care and transition support would pull residents and dollars away from facilities.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and personal care workforce
industries.note: The bill routes new Medicaid dollars through agency-provider and consumer-directed models, creating a permanent home-based channel for long-term care, and funds activities to raise home care workers' skills, earnings, and career prospects. Consumers gain independence at the same time the home care sector becomes the default provider.
States would gain enhanced federal matching funds for early adoption but take on a mandatory statewide benefit, new quality assurance systems, and maintenance-of-effort obligations.
